html:
The Trucial States were the sheikhdoms on the southern shore of the Persian Gulf, such as Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Sharjah, that signed treaties with Britain between 1820 and 1892. The map shows them from 1880 to 1938.

Britain wanted safe seas for its ships to India. After attacking the Al Qasimi ports in 1819, it made the sheikhs sign the General Maritime Treaty of 1820, then a permanent truce at sea in 1853, which gave the coast its name. In 1892 the sheikhs agreed to deal with no foreign power except Britain. Britain ran their foreign affairs, through the government of British India, and left them to rule at home.

Life rested on fishing, trade and above all pearl diving. When Japanese cultured pearls and the Great Depression hit the pearl market around 1930, the coast grew poor. Oil found in Abu Dhabi in 1958 changed everything. When Britain left in 1971, six of the sheikhdoms formed the United Arab Emirates, and Ras al-Khaimah joined in 1972.
